part 1/1: [source_identity] "who is loved with an affection of supernatural love" vs "propter Deum ex affectu amoris supernaturalis dilectum": Latin has 'on account of God from affection of supernatural love [having been] loved' — the English makes 'who is loved' a relative clause about God, but the Latin 'dilectum' is a past participle agreeing with 'Deum' as object of the preposition 'propter', not a finite verb 'who is loved'. [as one] loved', not 'on account of God, who is loved'.; [completeness] "That sorrow is true contrition" vs "qui est vera contritio": English adds 'That sorrow' as subject, but Latin 'qui' (masculine) refers back to 'Deum... dilectum' or the whole preceding clause, not 'dolor' (masculine could match, but the antecedent is ambiguous).
